```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cfisher)
fmt_p <- function(p) format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 1e-4)
```

## The problem

The classic Fisher's exact test tests whether a binary exposure and a binary outcome are
associated by providing an exact p-value even when counts are small. However, it does not
control for confounders. When extra variables influence both the exposure and the outcome,
the false positive rate of the test is inflated by the spurious association caused by these
confounders.

The usual remedy is a logistic regression of the outcome on the exposure and the
confounders. However, its p-values rest on large-sample approximations. They can be unreliable
when the exposure is rare, when the number of cases is small, or when the data show
(quasi-)separation, in which case the fitted coefficient of the exposure diverges.

`cfisher.test()` keeps the exactness of Fisher's exact test and adds the control for
confounders. The p-value and the interval are exact at the true slopes of the confounders
and approximate at the fitted ones. For the odds ratio the slopes are refitted under each
hypothesized odds ratio, a plug-in whose coverage was checked in a simulation reported in
the accompanying paper (Wu and Contador, 2026, a draft).

## What the test does

Fit a logistic model of the outcome `y` on the confounders `z`, without the exposure
`x`. Under the null hypothesis that the exposure does not matter given the confounders,
this model gives every subject's probability of being a case. The test statistic is $T$,
the number of cases among the exposed subjects. Its exact null distribution follows from
those probabilities.

* With `conditional = TRUE` (the default), the number of exposed subjects and the number
  of cases are both held fixed, as in Fisher's exact test. The null distribution of $T$ is
  then the conditional Bernoulli distribution, which reduces to the hypergeometric
  distribution when all subjects have the same probability. Without confounders the
  function returns the results of `fisher.test()`.
* With `conditional = FALSE`, only the exposed subjects are held fixed, and the null
  distribution is the Poisson-binomial distribution of $T$. Without confounders, the
  unconditional test does not reduce to `fisher.test()`.

The function also returns the odds ratio of the exposure given the confounders with a
confidence interval. For each hypothesized odds ratio, the slopes of the confounders are
refitted by maximum likelihood with the exposure term as an offset, the null distribution
of $T$ is recomputed at the resulting probabilities, and the test is inverted. The refit is
needed because the null model, fitted without the exposure, absorbs part of the exposure
effect when the exposure is common. When `fit` is a vector of probabilities, the slopes
cannot be refitted and the odds ratio uses the exponential tilt of the distribution at
those probabilities, which is exact only when they are the baseline probabilities under the
alternative.

## An example with a confounder

We simulate a confounder `z` that raises both the chance of exposure and the chance of
being a case. The exposure itself has no effect on the outcome.

```{r data}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 600
z <- rnorm(n)
x <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1 + 1.2 * z))   # the confounder raises exposure
y <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 1.0 * z)) # the confounder raises risk; x has no effect
table(exposure = x, outcome = y)
```

Fisher's exact test ignores `z`.

```{r fisher}
ft <- fisher.test(table(x, y))
ft
```

```{r cf}
cf <- cfisher.test(x, y, z)
cf
```

```{r numbers, include = FALSE}
p_unadj <- ft$p.value
p_adj <- cf$p.value
verdict <- function(p) if (p < 0.05) "rejects" else "does not reject"
```

At the 5% level, the unadjusted test `r verdict(p_unadj)` the null hypothesis
(p-value `r fmt_p(p_unadj)`, estimated odds ratio `r round(unname(ft$estimate), 2)`), and
the test that controls for `z` `r verdict(p_adj)` it (p-value `r fmt_p(p_adj)`, estimated
conditional odds ratio `r round(unname(cf$estimate), 2)`, 95% confidence interval from
`r round(cf$conf.int[1], 2)` to `r round(cf$conf.int[2], 2)`). The exposure has no effect
in this simulation, so a rejection by the unadjusted test is an association created by the
confounder.

## Reading the output

The printed result is an `htest` object, so it prints like the output of `fisher.test()`.

* `T` is the observed number of exposed cases, and `exposed`, `cases` and `n` give the
  number of exposed subjects, of cases and of subjects.
* The alternative `"two.sided"` is the default. `"greater"` tests whether the exposed are
  enriched among the cases, and `"less"` whether they are depleted.
* The estimate is the odds ratio of the exposure given the confounders. The confidence
  interval inverts the two tails of the null distribution at half the error probability
  each, with the slopes refitted at each hypothesized odds ratio. It is `0` or `Inf` at an
  end when the observed count is at an end of the support.
* `midp = TRUE` returns the mid-p value, which counts the observed count with half its
  probability. The estimate and the interval do not change.
* The components `null.distribution` and `expected` hold the null distribution of $T$
  that the test used and its mean. The expected number of exposed cases here is
  `r round(cf$expected, 1)`, against `r unname(cf$statistic)` observed.

```{r nulldist}
head(cf$null.distribution)
```

`cfisher.null()` returns the same distribution without running the test, for use in other
software that takes a discrete null distribution.

## Scanning many exposures against one outcome

In a genome-wide scan, thousands of binary variants (exposures) are tested against one
outcome. The null model does not contain the exposure, so it is the same for every
variant. Fit it once and pass it with `fit`, which can be a binomial `glm` or a vector of
probabilities.

```{r scan}
fit <- glm(y ~ z, family = binomial)
variants <- sapply(c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20), function(f) rbinom(n, 1, plogis(qlogis(f) + 0.8 * z)))
colnames(variants) <- paste0("variant", 1:4)
scan_p <- apply(variants, 2, function(v) cfisher.test(v, y, fit = fit, conf.int = FALSE)$p.value)
signif(scan_p, 3)
```

Setting `conf.int = FALSE` skips the estimate and the interval (unlike `fisher.test()`,
which still returns its estimate), which saves time when only p-values are needed. The cost
of one test grows with the product of the number of subjects and the number of cases.

## The unconditional option

`conditional = FALSE` does not hold the number of cases fixed. Its null distribution is the
Poisson-binomial distribution of the exposed subjects' null probabilities, which is the null
of the BinomiRare test (Sofer, 2017) and of the conditional randomization test
(Cand&egrave;s et al., 2018). The conditional option is the generalization of Fisher's exact
test, and it is the default.

```{r uncond}
p_cond <- cfisher.test(x, y, fit = fit)$p.value
p_unc <- cfisher.test(x, y, fit = fit, conditional = FALSE)$p.value
```

On the example above the two-sided p-value is `r fmt_p(p_cond)` with the conditional null and
`r fmt_p(p_unc)` with the unconditional one.

Sofer, T. (2017). BinomiRare: A robust test of the association of a rare variant with a
disease for pooled analysis and meta-analysis, with application to the HCHS/SOL. *Genetic
Epidemiology*, 41(5), 388-395. <https://doi.org/10.1002/gepi.22044>

Wu, Z. and Contador, G. (2026). Fisher's exact test controlling for confounders. Draft
